extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, policy makers, administrative law scholars, and congressional staff concerned with national-security sanctions and procedural due process
extracted.subtask_description: A law-review comment arguing Congress should amend IEEPA to impose statutory procedural requirements on Executive-branch regulations (particularly OFAC/State SDGT designations and asset-blocking) to better balance national-security interests and affected entities' due process rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codify procedural requirements in IEEPA
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should amend IEEPA (e.g., add a new provision to §203/50 U.S.C. §1702) to mandate certain procedural requirements that Presidential regulations must meet when they affect persons or groups present in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codifying necessary procedural requirements in a statute would allow the Executive Branch to continue to exercise discretion while limiting that discretion by specified procedural safeguards; such codification would give Congress complete control over the process and constrain Executive flexibility (analogy to AEDPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a post-deprivation statement of reasons concurrent with notification
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies implementing IEEPA-based regulations, including OFAC and the Department of State, should provide affected entities with a post-deprivation statement of reasons for a designation decision or blocking order, and that statement should be provided concurrently with notification of intent to designate or block assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require an unclassified summary of the reasons behind designation/blocking and a realistic way to respond to that information; concurrent notification would prevent multi-year asset freezes without a final decision and would give entities a more meaningful opportunity to challenge the action (comparison to FTO protections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a post-deprivation hearing before a neutral decisionmaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations should guarantee affected entities a post-deprivation hearing before a neutral decisionmaker (which could be the OFAC Director or a delegate) as the opportunity to present evidence and challenge blocking or designation decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process does not always require pre-deprivation hearings where extraordinary circumstances (e.g., asset flight risk) exist—Mathews v. Eldridge supports post-deprivation procedures; hearings could take the form of a mandatory meeting with the Director or delegate; Withrow permits an agency head to hear evidence and still serve as a neutral decisionmaker, subject to judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require the OFAC Director to meet with and respond to challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director of OFAC should be required (not left to discretion) to meet with an entity challenging either the blocking of its assets or its final designation as an SDGT, and to respond to the entity's challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current regulations allow the Director to meet at his discretion (31 C.F.R. §501.807(c)); mandatory meetings and responses help ensure the right to be heard and may allow entities to avoid final designation by challenging an initial blocking order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide affected entities a realistic way to respond to classified information
rubrics_metrics.description: When designations rely on classified information, the agency must provide an unclassified summary and a realistic means for the entity to respond to the basis for the designation or blocking order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unclassified summary and response opportunity help limit OFAC's ability to impose harsh sanctions on entities linked only indirectly to terrorism and enable meaningful challenges; this mirrors protections given to FTOs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow limited judicial review in the D.C. Circuit of hearing outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Entities should have an option for judicial review in the D.C. Circuit of the outcome of their informal/institutional hearing with OFAC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting review in the courts of appeals (D.C. Circuit) imposes a similar standard to AEDPA review and comports with judicial-economy practices favoring appeals-court review; scope of review should be limited to APA §706 grounds (arbitrary and capricious, abuse of discretion, statutory violation, constitutional violations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope of judicial review to standard APA/ statutory/constitutional grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review of agency action arising from hearings should be limited to analyses of whether OFAC's actions were arbitrary and capricious, an abuse of discretion, in excess of statutory authority, or incompatible with due process/constitutional rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A),(C)–(D); mandating procedural protections reduces incentives to assert other theories (e.g., §706(2)(B) 'contrary to constitutional right') because procedures will protect constitutional rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit new procedural protections to entities with a U.S. presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any statutory amendment should be limited to regulating agencies' actions as to individuals or entities present in the United States (codified at 50 U.S.C. §1702(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting the amendment to entities with U.S. presence is simpler and reflects that entities without U.S. connections have limited due process rights; avoids complexities of extraterritorial application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow agencies to retain substantive discretion while imposing procedural limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendment should permit the Executive Branch to continue exercising discretionary national-security decisions (e.g., designations under Exec. Order No. 13,224) while conditioning that discretion on required procedures (notice, hearing, review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies could still designate SDGTs or block assets based on financial/other support to terrorists, but must follow prescribed procedural steps so that entities receive notice and chance to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-deprivation hearing (not full evidentiary) is appropriate given asset-flight risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the primary consequence of SDGT designation is asset-blocking and entities may transfer assets abroad, due process may be satisfied by a post-deprivation hearing rather than a pre-deprivation full evidentiary hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathews balancing and precedent (e.g., Calero Toledo and Ninth Circuit cases) support that extraordinary situations permit withholding pre-deprivation hearings when necessary to protect compelling interests and ensure speed of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the same procedural standards to Department of State SDGT designations because OFAC controls financial assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Department of State's designations involve different discretionary issues, the Department's SDGT designations should be governed by the same standards as OFAC's because OFAC ultimately controls the financial assets of all designated SDGTs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform standards across agencies reduce disparity in consequences based on which agency designates an entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title VII: 'because of sex' includes sex stereotyping (Price Waterhouse standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Title VII's prohibition on discrimination 'because of sex' covers sex stereotyping: an employer who acts on the basis of beliefs about how men or women should behave is acting on the basis of gender in violation of Title VII.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price Waterhouse held that treating an employee differently for failing to conform to gender norms (e.g., feminine behavior) is discrimination 'because of sex'—employers may not take gender into account when making employment decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macy: transgender claims cognizable under sex stereotyping and per se 'taking gender into account' theory
rubrics_metrics.description: EEOC's decision in Macy recognizes that transgender individuals can bring claims under both a sex-stereotyping theory and a theory that any employment action that 'takes gender into account' is per se sex discrimination under Title VII.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macy extends Hopkins' reasoning and supports the position that discrimination against transgender persons (and, by extension, sexual-orientation-related stereotyping) falls within Title VII's protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: EEOC should issue written guidance that sexual orientation discrimination falls under Title VII
rubrics_metrics.description: The EEOC should issue guidance making clear that Title VII's prohibition on discrimination 'because of sex' includes discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, both as sex stereotyping and as per se 'taking gender into account' per Macy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official EEOC guidance is necessary to ensure uniform application and implementation of Title VII consistent with Macy; while the EEOC has nonbinding decisions recognizing sexual-orientation claims as sex stereotyping, it has not issued comparable binding guidance.
